feedback: When a child applies an operation to the two given numbers automatically, without checking the story (e.g. trying 7 − 9 or 9 − 7 for 7 = ? − 9), redirect to the story structure with a question rather than giving the answer.
Follow the child's approach and ask for justification; adapt prompts to whether they are stuck on parsing '=' or on choosing the operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning aloud about knowns and the unknown can develop the modelling and inverse reasoning needed for harder problem structures.
learnerActions: Respond to a coach who asks you to name what is known and what is unknown in a problem.
Justify which operation you will use and where the unknown sits, especially for start-unknown and missing-number problems.
Talk through 7 = ? − 9: identify that you need a starting number which, after removing 9, leaves 7.
activities.title: Coaching dialogue: 'What do we know, what are we finding?'

feedback: If a child answers 7 = ▢ − 9 as 7 − 9 or refuses, return to the bar model: whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 16.

If a child subtracts on a take-away start-unknown problem (e.g. 'I had some, ate 9, 7 are left'), have them act it out to see that the start was larger than what remained. (On an add-on start-unknown problem such as 'I had some, got 5 more, now I have 12', subtracting 12 − 5 is correct.)
activities.intendedInsight: Problems with the unknown in varied positions require the same modelling reasoning; recognising the structure matters more than the keyword.
learnerActions: Fill in equations with the unknown in different positions, e.g. 7 = ▢ − 9, ▢ + 5 = 12, 12 − ▢ = 8.
Answer word problems with picture support where the unknown is the result, change or start.
Mark which problems were 'find the start' problems rather than 'find what's left'.
activities.title: Missing-number and word-problem practice set
